methods.label: Subtract the white regions
methods.explanation:
Compare each shaded area by subtracting its white regions from the surrounding shape. Use the packet's recorded convention that the depicted inscribed and tangent configurations are exact. Let \(S_A,S_B,S_C\) denote the shaded areas in square centimeters.

[Figure 1](figures/2003_AMC_8_Q22_question_fig1.svg)

In \(A\), the square has side \(2\), and its inscribed circle has radius \(1\). Hence
\[
S_A=2^2-\pi\cdot1^2=4-\pi.
\]
For \(B\), it suffices to show that the total white area is at least \(\pi\). Let the positive diameters of the top two circles, measured in centimeters, be \(p\) and \(q\). Their horizontal spans cover the square's width: one circle reaches the left side, the other reaches the right side, and they touch. Consequently \(p+q\ge2\). Expanding squares gives
\[
p^2+q^2=\frac{(p+q)^2+(p-q)^2}{2}\ge2.
\]
Their combined area is therefore at least \(\pi(p^2+q^2)/4\ge\pi/2\). The same reasoning applies to the bottom two circles. Since the four white circles have disjoint interiors, their total area is at least \(\pi\), giving
\[
S_B\le4-\pi=S_A.
\]
In \(C\), the outer circle has radius \(1\). Each diagonal of the inscribed square is a diameter of length \(2\). The square's diagonals bisect each other at right angles, dividing it into four right triangles with perpendicular legs \(1\). Thus the white square has area \(4(1\cdot1/2)=2\), and
\[
S_C=\pi-2.
\]
Finally,
\[
S_C-S_A=2(\pi-3)>0
\]
because \(\pi>3\). Therefore figure \(C\) has more shaded area than either other figure, so the answer is \(\boxed{C}\).
